title: How well does an LLM-style coder count negative emotion in real comments, and does the correction still pay?
summary: The Claude session agent coded 300 real GoEmotions comments (blind to the human labels, one pass; not an API-called model) and over-coded: 132 flagged against 70 by raters, sensitivity 0.81, specificity 0.67, kappa 0.37, so the naive prevalence is 0.44 against a true 0.23 (coverage 0). That is the opposite error from the naive-Bayes and word-list stand-ins of qual-real, which undercount by 10 points. Its accuracy (0.71) is indistinguishable from naive Bayes (exact McNemar p = 0.4) and worse than a 38-word list (0.84, p = 0.0001). Its error differs by comment length (sensitivity 0.95 short, 0.76 long), but prediction-powered inference stays valid (bias under 0.006, coverage 0.96–0.996) and was 29% wider than hand-coding alone at 60 hand-coded items. Limits: one reader and pass, codebook mismatch with the raters' 11-emotion majority, possible dataset exposure, and a 300-item corpus that makes intervals conservative.
lede: how well does an LLM-style coder count negative emotion in real comments? The Claude session agent, coding 300 GoEmotions comments blind, flags 44% as negative against a human 23% (opposite error to the classical stand-ins); accuracy 0.71 matches naive Bayes and trails a word list, and prediction-powered inference stays valid but 29% wider than hand-coding. One reader, not an API model.
